levels.title: Good Guess, Bad Guess
levels.story: Rowan sets a stopwatch on a stump. "Run the delivery twice," says Rowan. "Once with no guess, once with a guess. Watch how many states you look at." Kit scribbles a number after each run.

everyday.scene: A sat-nav does not try every road. It picks roads that seem to head towards your destination, using a rough estimate of how far is left.
everyday.question: How can a planner tell which state is closer to the goal when there is no map?
everyday.answer: It works out a rough estimate from the facts, such as counting the goal facts that are not yet true, and explores the states with the lowest estimate first.

lessons.title: A quick estimate
text: A heuristic is a quick estimate of how far a state is from the goal. A search uses it to try the promising states first. It trades some certainty for speed.
On a map you can measure distance with a ruler. A planning state is only a set of facts, so the estimate has to be worked out from those facts alone.

terms.meaning: A quick estimate used to guide a search.

lessons.title: Counting unmet goals
text: One simple estimate works on any STRIPS problem: count the goal facts that are not yet true. At the start of Kit's delivery both goals are missing, so h is 2. After 'drop p at Dock' only 'q at Cabin' is missing, so h is 1.
In one test run, with ties settled by the order the actions are listed, plain breadth-first search looked at 37 states. A* with this guess looked at 23, and both found the 8-action plan.

lessons.title: Weak, strong, or too bold
text: A guess of 0 gives no help. A guess close to the true cost helps a lot. A guess that is too high can send A* the wrong way. Goal counting is a safe low guess in Kit's world, because each action adds at most one goal fact.
It would overestimate if one action could make two goals true at once. Imagine a 'drop both parcels' action. With two goals missing the count says 2, yet only 1 action is left.

deeper.title: Better guesses
text: Counting goals is crude because it ignores how hard each goal is to reach. The next level builds a guess that follows what it would actually take.

activities.prompt: Match each heuristic idea to its description.

pairs.right: Counts goal facts not yet true
Higher than the real cost, can mislead A*
Never higher than the real cost

hints: One of these is a safe guess.
One of these is a danger.
activities.explain: A zero guess does not help, goal count is one real guess, an overestimate can mislead, and admissible guesses never go too high.

activities.prompt: Is each guess safe (never too high) or risky (may be too high)?

items.text: The exact number of actions left
A guess of 0 for every state
Goal count when one action can finish two goals at once
A guess of 50 when every plan has 8 actions or fewer

hints: Safe means never above the real cost.
activities.explain: Exact and zero guesses never go too high. Goal count with a two-goals-at-once action, or a huge number, can.

activities.prompt: Kit is at the Dock, and both p and q are at the Dock. The goal is p at Dock and q at Cabin. What is h?
hints: Which goal fact is already true?
activities.explain: 'p at Dock' is true and 'q at Cabin' is not, so h = 1.

activities.prompt: Which guess helps the search most?

options.text: One close to the true remaining cost without going above it

hints: A good guess tells the search which states are closer.
Going above the true cost can mislead A*.
activities.explain: A guess near the truth steers A* well, and staying at or below it keeps the answer a cheapest plan.

activities.prompt: Challenge: in the state with Kit, p and q all at the Dock, h is 1 but the true shortest plan to the goal has 4 actions. By how much does h underestimate?
hints: Subtract h from the true plan length.
activities.explain: The true plan needs 4 actions and h is 1, so h is 3 too low. That is safe, but not very informative.

activities.prompt: Challenge: a 'drop both parcels' action could finish both goals at once. With both goals missing, goal count says 2. What does that do?

options.text: It overestimates: only 1 action is left

hints: Compare 2 with the actions really left.
A guess above the real cost is an overestimate.
activities.explain: One action is enough, but the count says 2, so the guess is too high.

fieldNotes.title: Heuristics
fieldNotes.text: A heuristic trades optimality, completeness, accuracy or precision for speed. A heuristic function ranks the choices in a search at each branching step.

fieldNotes.title: Admissible guesses
fieldNotes.text: A heuristic is admissible if it never overestimates the cost of reaching the goal.

fieldNotes.title: Forward search with heuristics
fieldNotes.text: Classical planning can be done by forward state-space search, possibly improved with heuristics.

summary: You met heuristics, used the goal count as a guess, saw it stay at or below the true remaining cost, and learned why a guess that is too high can mislead A*.
Rowan checks the stopwatch. "Twenty-three, against thirty-seven." Kit grins. "A rough guess already helps. A cleverer one might help more."

mistake.title: Trusting an overestimate
mistake.text: A guess that is higher than the true cost can make A* skip the best plan. Staying at or below the truth keeps the answer a cheapest one.
